common_name: Laura Bush Petunia (Heat-Tolerant Texas Superstar Petunia)

planting.note: Set out transplants after last frost; Laura Bush is a Texas Superstar-designated petunia selected for outstanding heat and humidity tolerance and a self-cleaning habit, blooming through summer conditions that cause most bedding petunias to collapse.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil after the danger of frost has passed, spacing plants 10-14 inches apart. Laura Bush is a naturally occurring petunia selection discovered in Texas and named for the former First Lady, then trialed and designated a Texas Superstar by Texas A&M AgriLife Extension for exceptional performance in Texas heat, humidity, and alkaline soil where hybrid bedding petunias typically decline by midsummer. Unlike most petunias, it is self-cleaning — spent flowers drop away on their own without deadheading — and it reseeds readily, often returning the following year in mild-winter zones. Flowers are smaller than hybrid petunias, in shades of light purple to lavender, but are produced in such profusion that the plant is smothered in bloom from spring through fall. It tolerates poor, alkaline soil and considerable drought once established, needing far less water and fertilizer than typical bedding petunias. Shear back by about a third in midsummer if plants become leggy to encourage fresh, compact regrowth for fall bloom.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Program: Laura Bush Petunia
Aggie Horticulture — Heat-Tolerant Bedding Plants for Texas

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in any moist to dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Katie is a compact, largely sterile dwarf selection of Mexican petunia bred to spread far less aggressively than the straight species, making it the recommended choice for residential borders and edging where the full-sized species can become a spreading nuisance.

directions: Plant in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 10-14 inches apart for a solid groundcover effect. Katie is a dwarf cultivar of Mexican petunia, staying under a foot tall compared to the species' 2-4 foot height, and is prized as the responsible choice for Gulf Coast gardeners who want the plant's nonstop purple bloom and toughness without its tendency to spread aggressively by runners and self-sown seed — the straight species is considered invasive in natural areas across Florida and other Gulf states. Each funnel-shaped purple flower lasts only a single day, but the compact, well-branched clumps produce so many buds that bloom appears continuous from spring through frost. It is remarkably heat, drought, and salt tolerant once established, tolerating conditions that stress most other low-growing perennials, and works well as a dense edging plant, in mass plantings, or in containers. Shear back by about a third in mid-season if plants become leggy to refresh the display.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Ruellia simplex Cultivar Comparison

common_name: Gold Star Esperanza (Cold-Hardy Compact Yellow Bells)

planting.note: Set out transplants after last frost in full sun in well-drained, lean, alkaline-tolerant soil; Gold Star was selected for improved cold hardiness and a more compact habit than standard yellow bells, allowing roots to survive winters as cold as zone 7b-8a where the species itself typically needs zone 8b or warmer to reliably return.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, alkaline-tolerant soil after the danger of frost has passed. Gold Star is a selection of esperanza (yellow bells) chosen for a more cold-hardy root system and a more compact, better-branched habit than the standard species, which lets gardeners in zone 7b and 8a grow it as a reliable perennial that dies back to the ground and resprouts each spring, rather than needing to treat it as a tender annual or overwinter it indoors. It produces the same masses of bright golden-yellow, trumpet-shaped, hummingbird-attracting flowers from early summer through the first hard frost, but on a shrub that typically stays a more manageable 4-6 feet rather than the 8-12 feet the straight species can reach in zone 9-11. In milder zones it remains semi-evergreen; where winters kill the top growth, cut the dead stems back to the ground in late winter and the plant resprouts vigorously and blooms the same season. Prune to shape in early spring to encourage the most compact, floriferous growth.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Program: Gold Star Esperanza
Oklahoma State University Extension — Tecoma stans in Southern Gardens

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing at least 18 inches apart for air circulation; Fanick's Phlox was discovered thriving in a San Antonio, Texas, nursery where standard garden phlox cultivars had failed, and it is one of the few tall garden phlox selections that reliably survives as a true perennial through Gulf South summer heat and humidity.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation. Fanick's Phlox was discovered as a chance seedling at Fanick's Garden Center in San Antonio, Texas, where it persisted and thrived for years despite the intense summer heat that typically causes garden phlox (Phlox paniculata) to decline or succumb to powdery mildew within a season or two in the South. Texas A&M AgriLife Extension trials confirmed its outstanding heat tolerance and disease resistance relative to standard garden phlox cultivars, and it was subsequently promoted as one of the few tall phlox reliably perennial in zone 8-9 gardens. It produces large, fragrant clusters of soft lavender-pink flowers from early summer into fall, attracting butterflies and hummingbirds, on sturdy, upright stems that hold up well without staking. Divide congested clumps every 3-4 years in early spring to maintain vigor, and deadhead spent flower heads to prolong bloom and prevent excessive self-seeding.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Fanick's Phlox Performance Trials

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after last frost in well-drained soil; Marbrite is an Italian fig variety valued for its pale green skin and sweet, amber-white flesh, offering a distinct fresh-eating alternative to the pink- and red-fleshed figs most common in Gulf Coast gardens.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun. Marbrite is an Italian fig cultivar bearing medium-sized figs with pale green to yellow-green skin and sweet, translucent amber to white flesh, a lighter-colored departure from the deep pink and red interiors of Gulf Coast standards like Celeste and Brown Turkey. It typically produces two crops in warm climates: a smaller breba crop on overwintered wood in early summer, followed by a larger main crop on new growth from midsummer into fall. Figs fruit on both second-year wood and current-season growth, so avoid heavy winter pruning, which removes the breba crop; light shaping after the main harvest is sufficient. Trees are vigorous and productive once established and rarely need fertilizer, though a layer of mulch over the root zone helps in zone 7-8 where occasional hard freezes can damage unprotected roots. Harvest when fruit softens and the neck bends over, since figs do not ripen further once picked.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Fig Variety Descriptions
